title: The kitchen door stays open
hook: langar is free to anyone of any background, in many gurdwaras all day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pangat, the row on the floor where no one sits higher. Your line was same row. Did you eat one meal sitting low? Day one hundred fifteen.

It's two in the afternoon on a Tuesday. You're a college student far from home, down to your last few dollars. Or a truck driver who's been on the road since four. Or someone who just lost a job and hasn't told anyone yet. You walk past a gurdwara, and someone at the door waves you in. You don't know a single word of Punjabi. You don't know what a Sikh believes. You're not sure you're allowed. You cover your head with a borrowed scarf, take off your shoes, sit down in the row, and a stranger puts hot food in your hands. Nobody asks your name. Nobody asks why you're hungry.
screen: `TWO IN THE AFTERNOON, TUESDAY.` → `WAVED IN AT THE DOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Langar is free, and it's for anyone. Any faith or none, any background, any reason for being hungry, or no reason at all. That's not a side rule. It's the whole point. In many gurdwaras the kitchen runs all day, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar it feeds tens of thousands of people every single day, around the clock. Remember the four doors of the Harmandir Sahib from day sixty? Doors facing every direction, so anyone from anywhere could walk in. The kitchen has the same shape. There's no ticket, no sermon you have to sit through first, no form to fill in. You do cover your head and take off your shoes, as everyone does. That's respect, not a test. Guru Nanak gives a picture in the Japji that fits the langar hall. In paraphrase: let wisdom be your food, and compassion the one who hands it out. And Sikhs have taken the open door far beyond the gurdwara. After floods and earthquakes, at borders, on highways where travelers are stranded, Sikh volunteers set up kitchens and start serving, often before anyone official arrives. The food is simple. The rule is the same. Here's what the open door asks of the people inside. Not just to cook, but to keep noticing who isn't in the room yet. The student. The driver. The person who's embarrassed to come. The door isn't really open if nobody ever walks out of it to wave someone in.
screen: `FREE, FOR ANYONE.` · `FOUR DOORS, ONE KITCHEN.` · `COMPASSION HANDS OUT THE FOOD.` · `NOTICE WHO ISN'T IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture the places you move through in a normal week: your street, your work, your school, the store, the bus. Now look, in your mind, for the people who might be hungry, or lonely at mealtimes. The new coworker who eats alone. The neighbor who lives by himself. The person you pass on the corner every day. Don't plan anything big yet. Just notice them. Let each face come, and stay a moment. The bell holds the time.
Langar. The Guru's kitchen, free to anyone, of any faith or none, no questions asked, in many places all day.
Your line: the door stays open. Today, notice one person near you who could use a meal, or company at one. Day one hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Langar is served free in every gurdwara to anyone who comes, and in many it runs all day; visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes, and Sikh volunteers also run langar kitchens at disasters and for travelers in need.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the Guru's kitchen, open to all.

trapdoor: what you thought: a free meal at a temple.
what it means: a kitchen whose door is open to anyone, so that no one has to explain their hunger.
what a scholar hears: the Japji's picture of wisdom as food and compassion as the one who serves it (stanza 29, Ang 6), and the Harmandir Sahib's doors open on all sides.

sources.ref: Japji Sahib, stanza 29, Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (wisdom as food, compassion as the one who serves it)
Sikh practice of langar in gurdwaras and in relief work

notes: Japji stanza 29 (bhugat gian daia bhandaran) paraphrased; confirm.
'Tens of thousands of people every single day, around the clock' at the Harmandir Sahib: common figures range 50,000-100,000 or more; confirm wording.
Sikh relief kitchens at disasters, borders and highways stated generally, no organization named. Confirm.
